parts.latex: What is the solution of the equation $\log_a x^3=b$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants?

solutions.latex:
Write the logarithm in index form:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_a x^3 &= b \\ x^3 &= a^b \\ x &= \left(a^b\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = a^{\frac{b}{3}} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Let $\log_a w=3, \log_a x=5$ and $\log_a y=7$ where $a>0$.

What is the value of $\log_a\left(\dfrac{w^2y}{x}\right)$?

solutions.latex:
Log laws:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_a\left(\dfrac{w^2y}{x}\right) &= 2\log_a w + \log_a y - \log_a x \\ &= 2\times 3 + 7 - 5 \\ &= 8 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve the equation given by $2\ln x=\ln(3-2x)$

solutions.latex:
We need $x > 0$ and $3 - 2x > 0$, so $0 < x < \dfrac{3}{2}$.

Using log laws, $2\ln x = \ln x^2$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \ln x^2 &= \ln(3 - 2x) \\ x^2 &= 3 - 2x \\ x^2 + 2x - 3 &= 0 \\ (x+3)(x-1) &= 0 \\ x &= 1 \text{ or } x = -3 \end{aligned}$$
$x = -3$ is rejected because $\ln(-3)$ is undefined.
$$\therefore\ x = 1$$
criteria: Solves the quadratic: $x=1$ or $x=-3$, or equivalent merit
Uses a log law to obtain $x^2=3-2x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the pair of simultaneous equations $\log_2 x+\log_2 y=3$ and $\log_x y=2$.

solutions.latex:
$\log_x y=2$, so $y=x^2$.

Then
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2 x+\log_2 y&=\log_2 xy\\ &=\log_2 x^3\\ &=3\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ x^3=2^3$

$\therefore\ x=2,\ y=4$

parts.latex: Evaluate $x$ when $x=\log_{31}32\times\log_{30}31\times\log_{29}30\times\ldots\times\log_2 3$ for $x\in\mathbb{Z}$.

solutions.latex:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$, to each factor:
$$x=\dfrac{\ln32}{\ln31}\times\dfrac{\ln31}{\ln30}\times\dfrac{\ln30}{\ln29}\times\cdots\times\dfrac{\ln4}{\ln3}\times\dfrac{\ln3}{\ln2}$$
Each numerator cancels with the next denominator, leaving
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{\ln32}{\ln2} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln2^5}{\ln2} \\ &= \dfrac{5\ln2}{\ln2} \\ &= 5 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the cancelling pattern, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $2e^k-5+2e^{-k}=0$.
Hence find in exact form any possible values of $k$.

solutions.latex:
Consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence have a common difference:
$$\begin{aligned}T_3-T_2&=T_2-T_1\\ 4e^k-5&=5-4e^{-k}\\ 4e^k-10+4e^{-k}&=0\\ 2e^k-5+2e^{-k}&=0\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Multiply by $e^k$ to form a quadratic in $e^k$:
$$\begin{aligned}2e^k-5+\dfrac{2}{e^k}&=0\\ 2e^{2k}-5e^k+2&=0\end{aligned}$$
Let $u=e^k$:
$$\begin{aligned}2u^2-5u+2&=0\\ (2u-1)(u-2)&=0\\ u&=\dfrac{1}{2},\ 2\\ e^k&=\dfrac{1}{2},\ 2\\ k&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right),\ \ln 2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Solves the quadratic in $u=e^k$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $\log_8 x+\log_4 x=5$.

solutions.latex:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}$, with base 2:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_8 x+\log_4 x&=5\\\dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 8}+\dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 4}&=5\\\dfrac{\log_2 x}{3}+\dfrac{\log_2 x}{2}&=5\\2\log_2 x+3\log_2 x&=30\\5\log_2 x&=30\\\log_2 x&=6\\x&=2^6\\&=64\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is equivalent to $\log_b\sqrt{c}$?

parts.latex: Given $\log_5 2=a$ and $\log_5 3=b$, express $\log_5\left(\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\log_2(1-x)+\log_2(3-x)=3$.

solutions.latex:
The logarithms need $1-x>0$ and $3-x>0$, so $x<1$.

Using the log law $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a(mn)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2[(1-x)(3-x)]&=3\\(1-x)(3-x)&=2^3\\x^2-4x+3&=8\\x^2-4x-5&=0\\(x-5)(x+1)&=0\\x&=5 \text{ or } x=-1\end{aligned}$$
$x=5$ does not satisfy $x<1$.
$$\therefore\ x=-1$$
criteria: Forms the correct quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equation $x^{\ln(2)}=8$.

solutions.latex:
Taking natural logs of both sides and using the log law $\ln a^n=n\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^{\ln 2}&=8\\ x^{\ln 2}&=2^3\\ \ln\left(x^{\ln 2}\right)&=\ln\left(2^3\right)\\ \ln 2\,\ln x&=3\ln 2\\ \ln x&=3\\ x&=e^3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the solution of the equation $x=\log_2 2\sqrt{2}+\log_2\sqrt{2}$?

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\log_a xy=\log_a x+\log_a y$ and $\log_a a=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\log_2 2+\log_2\sqrt{2}+\log_2\sqrt{2}\\ &=1+\log_2\left(\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}\right)\\ &=1+\log_2 2\\ &=1+1\\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$
Or:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\log_2\left(2\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}\right)\\ &=\log_2(2\times 2)\\ &=\log_2 2^2\\ &=2\log_2 2\\ &=2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given that $a=\log 5$ and $b=\log 2$, what is the expression of $\log 100$ in terms of $a$ and $b$?

Using the log laws $\log x^n=n\log x$ and $\log xy=\log x+\log y$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log 100&=\log 10^2\\ &=2\log 10\\ &=2(\log 2+\log 5)\\ &=2(a+b) \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Solve for $a$:

$$\ln(a)-\ln 3=\ln(a+2)-\ln(a-2)$$

solutions.latex:
Using the log law $\ln p-\ln q=\ln\dfrac{p}{q}$ on both sides:
$$\begin{aligned}\ln\left(\dfrac{a}{3}\right)&=\ln\left(\dfrac{a+2}{a-2}\right)\\ \dfrac{a}{3}&=\dfrac{a+2}{a-2}\\ a^2-2a&=3a+6\\ (a-6)(a+1)&=0\\ a&=6\text{ or } a=-1\end{aligned}$$
$\ln a$ needs $a>0$ and $\ln(a-2)$ needs $a>2$, so $a=-1$ is rejected.
$$\therefore a=6$$
criteria: Finds both answers correctly, or makes only one arithmetic mistake leading to two answers and rejects one, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}$ simplifies to $xy$.
Hence or otherwise, show that $\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Expanding and substituting the given $x^2+y^2=14xy$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{x^2+2xy+y^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{14xy+2xy}{16}\\&=\dfrac{16xy}{16}\\&=xy\end{aligned}$$

Using the log laws $\log a+\log b=\log ab$ and $n\log a=\log a^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\right)\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ LHS $=$ RHS, as required.

Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\sqrt{xy}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(x+y)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\log16\\&=\log(x+y)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}-\log16^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log(x+y)-\log4\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log x+\dfrac{1}{2}\log y\\&=\log x^{\frac{1}{2}}+\log y^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}\times y^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses any 2 relevant logarithm laws, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The expression $\dfrac{1}{\log_a(b)}+\dfrac{1}{\log_b(c)}+\dfrac{1}{\log_c(a)}$ is equal to

solutions.latex:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_b b}{\log_b a}$, to each term:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{\log_a(b)}+\dfrac{1}{\log_b(c)}+\dfrac{1}{\log_c(a)}&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{\log_b(b)}{\log_b(a)}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{\log_c(c)}{\log_c(b)}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{\log_a(a)}{\log_a(c)}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\log_b(a)}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\log_c(b)}}+\dfrac{1}{\frac{1}{\log_a(c)}}\\&=\log_b(a)+\log_c(b)+\log_a(c)\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve for $x$: $\log(3x+6)=\log 3+1$

e and natural logarithms.reason: log_e(x+2)=1 -> x+2=e is part of solving the log equation; base 10 also accepted.

Logarithm laws.reason: Assumed-algebra skill used only as a side step in the agreed Logarithmic equations.

solutions.latex:
Using base $e$ (the correct solution) and the log law $\ln a-\ln b=\ln\dfrac{a}{b}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_e(3x+6)-\log_e 3&=1\\\log_e\dfrac{3x+6}{3}&=1\\\log_e\dfrac{3(x+2)}{3}&=1\\\log_e(x+2)&=1\\x+2&=e^1\\x&=e-2\\x&\approx 0.72\ (2\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$
Using base 10 (also accepted):
$$\begin{aligned}\log_{10}(3x+6)-\log_{10}3&=1\\\log_{10}(x+2)&=1\\x+2&=10\\x&=8\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines the logs, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the solution(s) of the equation $\log_2(x-3)+\log_2 x=2$?

solutions.latex:
Both logarithms need a positive argument, so $x-3>0$ and $x>0$, giving $x>3$.

Using $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a mn$:

$$\begin{aligned} \log_2\left[(x-3)x\right] &= 2 \\ x^2-3x &= 2^2 \\ x^2-3x-4 &= 0 \\ (x-4)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=4$ or $x=-1$, but $x>3$.

Hence $x=4$ is the only solution.

parts.latex: What is the solution of the equation $\log_a x^4-\log_a x^2=b$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive?

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws, $\log_a x^n=n\log_a x$:

$$\begin{aligned} \log_a x^4-\log_a x^2 &= b \\ 4\log_a x-2\log_a x &= b \\ 2\log_a x &= b \\ \log_a x &= \dfrac{b}{2} \\ x &= a^{\frac{b}{2}} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given that $a=\log_2 7$ and $b=\log_7 16$, show that $ab=4$.

Using the change of base rule, $\log_7 16=\dfrac{\log_2 16}{\log_2 7}$:

$$\begin{aligned} ab &= \log_2 7\times\log_7 16 \\ &= \log_2 7\times\dfrac{\log_2 16}{\log_2 7} \\ &= \log_2 16 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes a correct change of base (or other log law that makes progress), or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Solve the equation:

$$\log_e(x+2)=\log_e(2x)$$

solutions.latex:
Both logarithms must be defined:
$$\begin{aligned}x+2&>0 &&\text{so } x>-2\\2x&>0 &&\text{so } x>0\end{aligned}$$
Together these give $x>0$.

Since the logarithms are equal, their arguments are equal:
$$\begin{aligned}x+2&=2x\\x&=2\end{aligned}$$
This satisfies $x>0$, so $x=2$.

parts.latex: If $log_a(xy^3)=1$ and $log_a(x^2y)=1$ what is the value of $log_a(xy)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\log_a(uv)=\log_a u+\log_a v$ and $\log_a u^n=n\log_a u$:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_a x+3\log_a y &= 1 &&(1) \\ 2\log_a x+\log_a y &= 1 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2\log_a x+6\log_a y &= 2 &&2\times(1) \\ 5\log_a y &= 1 &&(3)-(2) \\ \log_a y &= \dfrac{1}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\log_a x=1-3\log_a y=1-\dfrac{3}{5}=\dfrac{2}{5}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ \log_a(xy) &= \log_a x+\log_a y \\ &= \dfrac{1}{5}+\dfrac{2}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}$$
